newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright in Russia to talk NATO, arms control.
newsitem.headline: Albright in Russia to talk NATO, arms control.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived on Saturday for talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov to calm Moscow's fears over NATO expansion and push new arms control projects.

The pair, who have developed a considerable personal rapport despite their months of sometimes outspoken duelling over NATO expansion, are expected to try to put differences behind them now that NATO has announced its enlargement plans.

Primakov was on hand to meet Albright when she flew into St Petersburg's Pulkovo airport from Slovenia. They greeted each other with a handshake and kiss before being whisked off to the city. They made no statements to reporters.

Officials said Albright would brief Primakov over dinner on this week's NATO summit in Madrid, which invited three former communist nations -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- to apply to join.
Primakov on Tuesday called that move "the biggest mistake in Europe since the end of World War Two."
The officials said they also expected NATO's swoop on Thursday on suspected war criminals in Bosnia, which Russia denounced on Friday as "cowboy raids", would be discussed "at some length".

Arms control will be another key theme during Albright's 19-hour stay in the former tsarist capital, in which she will attempt to build on improving ties with Russia following the signing of a NATO-Russia charter in May.

Her visit, sandwiched between talks in would-be NATO members Slovenia and Lithuania, is part of a round of whistle-stop European tours by U.S. leaders including President Bill Clinton, following the Madrid summit.

It also opens a round of diplomatic house calls on Russia by Western foreign ministers. British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will be in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday. Germany's Klaus Kinkel will discuss NATO with Primakov on Tuesday in the capital.

All are expected to stress a willingness to develop cooperation between NATO and Moscow under the charter, which sought to allay Russia's fears over NATO expansion by giving it a say in alliance affairs and offering assurances on NATO deployment.
Russian officials, too, have pledged to enhance cooperation and not to dwell on their differences.

On her way into St Petersburg, the Czech-born Albright laid a wreath at a monument to the World War Two German siege of Leningrad -- as the city was then known -- and listened without an interpreter to the explanations of a guide.

She was then given a sneak preview of the interior of the newly restored Church on Spilt Blood, built on the site where Tsar Alexander II was assassinated in 1881. The church is to be opened to the public next month after being closed for years.
U.S. officials said Albright and Primakov would discuss 30-nation negotiations on updating a 1990 treaty limiting conventional arms in Europe and where they are deployed.
Answering a call Russia had made for years, the signatories agreed in December to review the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty to take account of the split of the Soviet Union.
Sluggish talks in Vienna have been given a new lease of life by the deal signed by Russia and NATO, and diplomats have said a new treaty could be ready early next year.

Russia made a key concession in May by agreeing to focus on national rather than "bloc" arms ceilings, but the officials said Moscow was still trying to limit the holdings of future new NATO states through five-yearly renegotiations.

Primakov and Albright were to talk over dinner at a restaurant and tour the Hermitage art gallery in the tsars' Winter Palace, seized by the Bolsheviks in their 1917 coup d'etat. On Sunday, they will talk over coffee at Albright's hotel before she flies on to Vilnius and Prague.
